frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1298:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff wrote jointly to the State Department and the British Foreign Office on 18 July 1945. The combined body spoke for both Western high commands at once. Addressing both foreign ministries in one letter matched that joint voice.

A letter of this kind carried the soldiers' shared view to the envoys of both nations. It bound the military and foreign arms of the alliance in a single text. This one dates from the summit's second day. It shows the joint staff speaking over the heads of the talks, straight to the two offices that would live with the peace.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1398:
A second Caffery letter to Foreign Minister Bidault dated 1 August 1945 follows in the volume. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Paired letters on one day often split a subject in two: one for the record, one for the harder point. Whatever the split here, the pace tells its own story. Paris and Washington were settling France's role in the postwar order at speed, while the ink dried at Potsdam. Readers following the Caffery and Bidault run get diplomacy at working level, where alliances are kept alive by prompt, exact paper rather than by speeches.
frus-1945-50-intel-d98:
Lyon, acting director of the State Department's Office of Controls, wrote to McCormack on 15 November 1945. The Office of Controls handled sensitive department business such as passports and visas. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

An approach from the controls office to the intelligence chief shows the seams where secret work touched the department's public duties. Names, travel, and papers crossed both desks, and the two offices had to agree on how to handle them. Readers gain a finer-grained picture of the State Department here than the top-level fight provides. The intelligence system was not only chiefs and plans; it was also clerks' questions about files, answered in memos like this one.
frus-1945-50-intel-d198:
Minutes record the Fourth Meeting of the National Intelligence Authority on 17 July 1946. It stands as document 198 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

Minutes are the formal record of a meeting: who sat in, what was put on the table, and what the group agreed to do. Read with the papers before and after it, the record shows a policy taking shape one meeting at a time. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d298: Dated 6 August 1948, "Memorandum of Conversation and Understanding" comes from the top level of the government. Readers meet it as document 298 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The Council had sent in an outside team to grade the CIA, and the whole town knew a blunt report was coming. A memorandum of conversation is the note a participant or aide wrote after a talk, setting down who was there and what was said.
frus-1945-50-intel-d398:
Fisher Howe, deputy to the State Department's intelligence chief, sent a memo to his boss, W. Park Armstrong, on 8 September 1949. The paper is document 398 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Howe and Armstrong led the Bureau of Intelligence and Research, the State Department's team of analysts. A deputy writing to his own chief is staff work at its most basic. Yet such notes set the line the bureau took when it faced the CIA and the military services across the table. The bureau's small staff punched far above its weight through notes of exactly this kind.
frus-1861-d98:
On 14 October 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote a second letter to Lord Lyons. It is document 98 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The paired letters of that day sort the Anglo American agenda into clean parts. Seward dealt with each point on its own paper, as was his habit. Together the two notes show a full day of work on the tie that mattered most to the Union. The two notes frame a single day of Anglo American business in full. A full day of such business shows how much of the war was fought in ink.
frus-1861-d198:
On 8 July 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Cassius Clay at the Russian court. The letter is document 198 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's July letter to St. Petersburg kept Clay inside the common plan. Even a friendly court had to hear the Union's terms in full. The note shows no post exempt from the Secretary's steady, central hand. No post exempt was Seward's rule, and the Russian file proves it page by page. Page by page proof of the rule is the quiet strength of this whole volume. No post stood outside the common plan.
frus-1861-d298:
Seward wrote again on 12 November 1861, this time to Mr. Robinson. It was printed as Document 298 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It was written in the autumn of the war's first year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d98:
Writing on 11 July 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London sent his report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 98 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d198:
Document 198 is a note from Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 4 January in the record of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It sits among the first papers of the new year in the British file.

Days earlier, Washington had agreed to give up the Confederate envoys taken from the Trent, and the crisis was cooling fast. Lyons stayed in close written touch with Seward as relations steadied. Notes from this turn of the year mark the point where the two governments stepped back from the edge of war. Cases under such notes were often small: one ship, one prisoner, one point of form.
frus-1862-d298:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 2 August 1862 in a letter printed as Document 298 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward, opening the August run of the French file.

August began with the Confederate raider Alabama newly escaped from Britain and French troops rebuilding strength in Mexico. Dayton's post touched both stories, since Paris coordinated loosely with London and owned the Mexican venture. His report that week fed Washington's picture of a Europe growing bolder as the Union's summer went badly. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d398:
On 14 January 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Horace J. Perry, the secretary of the American legation in Madrid. It opens the Spanish file as Document 398 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Spain held Cuba, close to the rebellious South, and had just sent troops to Mexico with Britain and France. Washington watched Madrid with care all through the war. Early orders like this one set the tone Perry was to keep at the Spanish court. He was to be firm on Union rights and calm in manner. He was also to watch for any sign that Spain might aid the Confederacy.
frus-1862-d498:
James Shepherd Pike closed April 1862 with a report from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 30 April. It is Document 498 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Pike's end-of-April letter caught the Dutch reaction to the war's improving Union news, including the fall of New Orleans. The Netherlands, with colonies in the West Indies, had to apply its neutrality rules to real ships in real ports. His reports touched those cases as they arose. For Seward, the Hague file was a steady source of European weather reports. For the reader, Pike's letters stand out in the volume for their plain speech and newsman's eye.
frus-1862-d598:
On 15 December 1861 Spain's minister of state addressed this instruction to General Prim, commander of the Spanish expeditionary force then sailing for Mexico. It is Document 598 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Prim was Spain's plenipotentiary as well as its general, charged with acting alongside Britain and France under their joint convention. Madrid's orders to him, printed here in translation, show what Spain said it wanted in Mexico: debts paid and order restored, not conquest. Read beside Corwin's reports from Mexico City, the letter lets the reader test Spanish words against Spanish conduct. The test runs through the months that followed. In them, Prim judged the French design and withdrew.
frus-1862-d698: On 5 September 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to a Mr. Yrisarri. The letter is document 698 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, answering Yrisarri's dispatch of late August. The evidence gives the two names and the date. It does not name Yrisarri's post or land, and the subject of the exchange is not stated.
frus-1863p1-d98:
On 2 March 1863, William H. Seward sent this letter to Charles Francis Adams, the second of twelve he sent him that day in this file. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 98 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Batch days like 2 March let Washington speak on many heads at once. Each head sat in its own sheet, so Adams could act on them one by one. The London brief held much to sort: claims, ships, talks, and tone. This letter holds one slice of that day's work. Its sense comes from the set it sits in, a full brief laid out in a row.
frus-1863p1-d198:
One of the Secretary's regular instructions to London, this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, is dated 9 May 1863. It appears as document 198 of the 1863 papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For readers today, these instructions reveal the thinking inside the State Department as clearly as any memoir. They show choices being made in real time, with poor information and high stakes. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d298:
On 22 September 1863, orders left Washington for London: Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The paper is document 298 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

The CSS Alabama, built near Liverpool, had slipped away in 1862 and was raiding Union trade. Washington pressed London to stop such ships and answer for the losses. It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d398:
One of Lord Lyons's regular notes to the State Department, this paper to Secretary of State William H. Seward is dated 19 February 1863. It appears as document 398 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Once emancipation became Union policy in January 1863, British protests grew harder to frame. Lyons had to press neutral rights for a government whose public mostly hated slavery. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d498:
8 May 1863 is the date on a letter from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d598:
A 1 August 1863 dispatch from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons reached Secretary of State William H. Seward. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the late summer of 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
plos-pbio-0020098:
György Hutvágner, Martin J. Simard, Craig C. Mello, and their group tested a way to block small RNAs in PLOS Biology in 2004. Small RNAs can silence specific genes, a process called RNA interference. The team used short custom molecules that pair with a chosen small RNA and stop it from working.

A clean off switch lets scientists ask what one small RNA does in a living animal. Without it, they can only add silencing, not remove a natural one. The method targets single RNA sequences with care, so side effects stay low. Tools like this helped turn small RNAs from a curiosity into a standard way to probe gene function across biology.
plos-pbio-0020198:
Kyra Oswald-Richter, Stacy M. Grill, Nikki Shariat, and their team examined regulatory T cells and HIV in PLOS Biology in 2004. Regulatory T cells calm the immune system. HIV can infect them, and can also infect normal T cells that have been reprogrammed to act like regulatory ones.

That dual route matters because regulatory cells sit at a control point of immunity. If HIV hides in them or copies their calming tricks, it may quiet the very response meant to fight it. The study maps both natural and reprogrammed cells as targets. Understanding this niche could help explain why HIV persists despite strong immune attacks, and where new therapies might aim.
plos-pbio-0020398:
Audrey P. Gasch, Alan M. Moses, Derek Y. Chiang, and their team compared gene control systems in fungi in PLOS Biology in 2004. Fungi in the ascomycete group include yeast and molds. Their genes are switched by binding sites near each gene, and those sites change as species evolve.

The team tracked how whole control systems were kept, rewired, or lost across these fungi. Some core systems stayed stable for hundreds of millions of years, while others turned over fast. That contrast shows evolution tinkers with control even when the genes themselves stay much the same. The work is a model for studying regulatory change, the part of evolution many now think drives most new traits.
plos-pone-0000098:
Claudia Arce, Carlos Pérez-Plasencia, Aurora González-Fierro, and their team ran an early clinical test in breast cancer in PLOS ONE in 2006. Epigenetic therapy uses drugs that switch silenced genes back on. The team added such therapy to standard chemotherapy given before surgery for locally advanced tumors.

A proof-of-principle study checks whether an idea works at all in patients, before large trials. The authors report the combined treatment could be given and showed signs of activity against the tumors. That green light is the true product of a small study like this. It justifies the cost and effort of proper trials to learn whether the benefit is real.
plos-pone-0000198:
Graham R. Martin, Kerry-Jayne Wilson, J. Martin Wild, and colleagues published this bird senses paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Kiwi are flightless, nocturnal birds from New Zealand that hunt by smell and touch. The authors report that kiwi forego vision in guiding their night activities, relying on their other senses instead.

Most birds are visual animals, so a bird that largely gives up sight is striking. The paper examines the kiwi's eyes and behavior to support that claim. It reframes the kiwi as a mammal-like bird, feeling its way through the dark forest floor. It also informs how this threatened species should be studied and protected.
plos-pone-0000298:
Tamara Glaser, Steven M. Pollard, Austin Smith, and colleagues published this stem cell paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Neural stem cells, called NS cells here, can be grown stuck to a dish and expanded over time. The authors demonstrate their tripotential differentiation: one cell line can produce all three main neural cell types, neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes.

A stem cell line is only useful if it keeps its full potential while expanding. Showing adherently grown NS cells stay tripotent validates them as a research tool. Such lines support work on brain development and on diseases where specific neural cells are lost.
plos-pone-0000398:
Inês Ribeiro and colleagues studied two genes that pace cell growth in the developing heart, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The genes, Tbx2 and Tbx3, belong to a family of developmental control genes. The team examined how they regulate the dynamics of cell proliferation, the rate at which heart cells multiply, during heart remodeling.

A growing heart must add cells fast enough to build the organ but stop in the right places to shape its chambers. Genes that set the pace of division help draw those boundaries. Understanding their control of heart growth bears on congenital heart defects, which often trace back to errors in these early patterning steps.
plos-pone-0000498:
Joy G. Ghosh, Scott A. Houck, and John I. Clark mapped the working surfaces of a lens chaperone protein, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Human αB crystallin is a molecular chaperone, a helper that keeps other proteins from clumping; in the eye lens it also provides structure. The team identified interactive domains in it that modulate microtubule assembly and disassembly.

Microtubules are the cell's rails and scaffolding, constantly built and taken apart. A chaperone that tunes that cycle connects protein quality control to cell architecture. αB crystallin also appears in brain and muscle. Its mutations cause cataract and muscle disease. So mapping its active regions has reach beyond the eye.
plos-pone-0000598:
Anouk C. Vedder and colleagues compared two replacement enzymes for a rare storage disease, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Fabry disease results from a missing enzyme that leaves fats to accumulate in organs. The comparative trial tested treatment with agalsidase alfa or beta at a dose of 0.2 mg/kg.

Two marketed versions of a therapy invite an obvious question: do they perform alike at the same dose? Head-to-head trials in rare diseases are hard to run because patients are few, making each one valuable. The outcome informs prescribing for a lifelong, expensive treatment.
plos-pone-0000698:
Magalie Lenoir, Fuschia Serre, Lauriane Cantin and colleagues compared the pull of sweetness with the pull of cocaine, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Refined sugars such as sucrose and fructose were absent from most diets until very recently in human history. Today, overconsumption of sugar-rich food helps drive the obesity epidemic. The team asked how strong sugar's reward really is.

Their title states the headline result: intense sweetness surpasses cocaine reward. In plain terms, the sweet option won over the drug option in their tests. A result like that reframes sugar from a soft pleasure to a powerful reward signal. It feeds debate about food design, addiction, and public health.
plos-pone-0000798:
Gerhard Kelter, Daniel Steinbach, Venkata Badireenath Konkimalla and colleagues asked why some tumor cells resist a malaria drug turned cancer drug. Artesunate exerts profound anti-cancer activity, and ferrous iron enhances tumor cells' susceptibility to it. The transferrin receptor, which imports iron by internalizing the carrier protein transferrin, is over-expressed in rapidly growing cells, including many tumors.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE study examines the transferrin receptor and two ABC transporters, ABCB6 and ABCB7, in resistance and differentiation of tumor cells toward artesunate. Transporters can pump drugs out or handle the iron that activates them. Knowing which proteins set sensitivity helps predict which tumors artesunate can treat.
plos-pone-0000898:
Hendrik de Jonge, Rudolf Fehrmann, Eveline de Bont and colleagues set out to choose housekeeping genes on evidence, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Gene studies need steady reference genes to make fair comparisons. The catch is that popular choices such as ACTB and GAPDH can swing widely between samples and conditions.

Unsteady references quietly corrupt results across whole fields. The team weighed candidates against data rather than habit, aiming for references that stay level. Their selection gives labs a safer base for measuring gene activity. The paper is a methods warning as much as a result: check your ruler before you measure.
plos-pone-0000998:
Alexander Sponner, Wolfram Vater, Shamci Monajembashi and colleagues unraveled the layered makeup of spider silk, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Silks are fairly well understood molecule by molecule. How those molecules are organized in layers inside a spun fiber, and what else the fiber contains, was much less clear.

The team linked defined structural elements in dragline silk from the spider Nephila clavipes to their molecular parts. Dragline silk is the famously strong thread spiders use as a lifeline. Mapping its hierarchy helps explain how soft proteins make a fiber tougher than steel by weight. That map also guides attempts to spin artificial silk.
plos-pone-0001098:
Keyue Ding, Samantha McDonough and Iftikhar Kullo found signs of positive selection in part of a cholesterol gene, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cholesterol balance is kept by tuned control of absorption, liver production and blood clearance. PCSK9, a secreted enzyme, is one of the controllers, and its variants move cholesterol levels strongly.

The team analyzed PCSK9 across fourteen primate species. Positive selection, change favored rather than merely tolerated, showed in the gene's C-terminal domain. Selection on a cholesterol controller hints at dietary pressures in primate history. It also flags which part of the protein evolution could not leave alone.
plos-pone-0001198:
Molecular chaperones help fold proteins inside cells, but they also circulate in the blood and can signal to immune cells. Alireza Shamaei-Tousi and colleagues measured these proteins in patients treated for periodontal disease, gum disease, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Evidence was emerging that chaperones exist in the circulation and can modulate white blood cell function.

The authors report differential regulation of circulating chaperone levels during treatment for periodontal disease. Gum disease is a chronic infection and inflammation, so it offers a window on how local disease affects body-wide signals. Their results connect oral health to the wider immune state.
plos-pone-0001298:
Between 2005 and 2050, the world's population is forecast to grow by 2.7 billion, mostly in low-income countries. Andrew Tatem and colleagues built high-resolution population maps for East Africa to help planners cope, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Census data alone are too coarse: they give totals for districts, not where people actually live.

The authors combined land cover data with census counts to distribute people across the landscape at fine resolution. Growth on that scale has social, economic, and environmental impacts. Maps like these guide where schools, clinics, vaccination campaigns, and aid should go.
plos-pone-0001398:
Daniel Rubio and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on stem cells that changed on their own in the lab. The team had earlier found that human stem cells from fat and marrow could turn into cells with tumor like traits. Here they mapped the gene shifts behind that change. Such maps are vital for safe use of stem cells in care.

By profiling the changed cells, they named the main gene and pathway shifts at work. The findings flag risks that clinics must screen for before transplants. They also show what to watch as cells are grown for long spans. That watch list can make stem cell cures safer for patients.
plos-pone-0001498:
Laura Forsberg White and Marcello Pagano published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the 1918 flu pandemic. That pandemic was the most deadly outbreak of the last century. With fresh fears of a new pandemic, its spread rate was worth a fresh count. The team used records from towns in Maryland and from two ships with well logged outbreaks.

From those close records they gauged how fast the 1918 virus passed from person to person. A firm rate from real data beats a guess from broad counts. It lets planners test control plans against a proven hard case. The work thus serves both history and future readiness.
plos-pone-0001598:
Sricharan Bandhakavi and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on yeast that resists a key drug. The drug rapamycin blocks the TOR path, a master growth switch in cells. Some yeast shrug the drug off. The team combined protein counts with gene tests to find how. They flagged a heat shock factor as a key player.

Switching that factor on both curbed resistance and dimmed TOR signals. That ties stress reply to growth control in a new way. TOR is a cancer drug target in people, so yeast clues carry weight. They may hint at how tumors dodge TOR drugs too.
plos-pone-0001698:
Jian Fu, Kathryn Fong, Alfonso Bellacosa, and their co-authors studied a tumor suppressor protein lost in lung cancer, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The protein is VILIP-1, part of a family of neuronal calcium sensors. In animal models it acts as a tumor suppressor, slowing cell growth, adhesion, and invasion in squamous cell carcinoma.

The team examined non-small cell lung carcinomas, the commonest lung cancers, to learn how VILIP-1 is turned down and whether its level predicts survival. The full text gives the tumor cell tests, the mechanisms of downregulation they found, and the survival analysis. A protein whose loss marks worse outcomes could guide prognosis, and restoring it is a possible treatment idea.
plos-pone-0001798:
Jonghwan Kim, Ji-hoon Lee, and Vishwanath R. Iyer mapped the target genes of a cancer-linked protein across the genome in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Myc is a transcription factor involved in many human cancers, and its overexpression is tied to malignant transformation. In normal cells Myc rises with growth signals and in turn regulates downstream genes.

Their global identification of Myc targets reveals a direct role in mitochondrial biogenesis, the building of new mitochondria. It also details how Myc uses its DNA binding motif in living cells. The full text gives the target list and validation tests. A growth switch that also orders more power plants explains part of how Myc fuels tumor growth.
plos-pone-0001898:
Branwen Hennig and co-authors asked why genes shape the response to the hepatitis B vaccine, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The vaccine is safe and works well, yet the level of protective proteins it raises fades with time. A high peak right after the shots means a slower fade and a lower risk of infection later.

The team looked for host gene traits that track with that peak level and with how fast it falls. Knowing which traits matter could help spot people who need extra shots. It also shows how much of vaccine success is set by the person, not just the dose. Such work can guide smarter vaccine plans.
plos-pone-0001998:
Pedro Martins, Fernando Rocha, and Ana Damas studied the physics of growing protein crystals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. To read a protein's shape, labs grow crystals of it, most often by vapor diffusion: a drop loses water slowly until crystals form. The rate at which water leaves the drop sets the quality of the crystals.

Past attempts to solve the math of that evaporation, by formula or by numbers, left gaps. The trio set out the basics of how water balance is reached in the setup. A rational grasp of the step could replace trial and error with design in crystal growth.
plos-pone-0002098:
Kamran Shalchian-Tabrizi and co-authors used many genes to redraw the tree at the root of animals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Animals are kin to fungi and to Choanozoa, mostly one-celled protozoans, in a great group called opisthokonts. To set the order of events when animals evolved from one-celled ancestors, the branches closest to that split must be right.

The team built a multigene phylogeny of Choanozoa and its kin. Many genes together can settle branches that single genes leave shaky. Knowing which living groups are animals' closest kin shows what the first animals inherited, and what they invented.
plos-pone-0002198:
Jason Rasgon proposed a new way to tell what a mosquito has fed on, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A mosquito that drinks blood can pass on malaria, dengue fever, and other diseases. Knowing which animals its blood came from helps trace how those diseases spread, but digestion destroys the meal fast. Current tests only work soon after feeding.

Rasgon suggests stable isotope analysis, which reads lasting chemical signatures in the mosquito's tissues. Those signatures can survive complete digestion of the blood meal. If the method holds up, disease teams could learn the feeding habits of caught mosquitoes long after the evidence would once have vanished.
plos-pone-0002298:
Jonathan FitzGerald, Ming Luo, and Abed Chaudhury tested a prediction about parent conflict in plant seeds, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The parental conflict idea says a mother plant restrains embryo growth while the father pushes it up, each serving their own genetic interest. In plants, the enzyme MET1, which places methyl marks on DNA, is a central regulator of the imprinted genes that tune seed growth.

The team asked how DNA methylation links the two parents' opposing pressures to actual embryo size. Their results show methylation causes predominantly maternal control of plant embryo growth. The finding refines how genetic conflict in seeds is understood at the molecular level.
plos-pone-0002398:
A research team led by Martin reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Bronwen Martin, Michele Pearson, Randall Brenneman, and others. Its subject is conserved and Differential Effects of Dietary Energy Intake on the Hippocampal Transcriptomes of Females and Males. The level of dietary energy intake influences metabolism, reproductive function, the development of age-related diseases, and even cognitive behavior.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002498:
Work from Hwang and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Nathaniel S. Hwang, Shyni Varghese, Jennifer Elisseeff, and others. Its subject is derivation of Chondrogenically-Committed Cells from Human Embryonic Cells for Cartilage Tissue Regeneration. Heterogeneous and uncontrolled differentiation of human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) in embryoid bodies (EBs) limits the potential use of hESCs for cell-based therapies.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002598:
In 2008, Valenzuela and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Michael J. Valenzuela, Perminder Sachdev, Wei Wen, and others. Its subject is lifespan Mental Activity Predicts Diminished Rate of Hippocampal Atrophy. Epidemiological studies suggest that complex mental activity may reduce the risk for dementia, however an underlying mechanism remains unclear.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002698:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by Sun-Chong Wang and colleagues addresses Age-Specific epigenetic drift in Late-Onset alzheimer's disease. The catalog record names Sun-Chong Wang first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Despite an enormous research effort. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002798:
Paolo Facella led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was diurnal and circadian rhythms in the tomato transcriptome and their modulation by cryptochrome photoreceptors. Authorship is credited in the record to Paolo Facella and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Circadian clocks are internal molecular time-keeping mechanisms that provide living organisms with the ability to adjust their growth and physiology and to anticipate diurnal. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002898:
Claudia Rübe, Jan Palm, Michael Erren and colleagues asked in 2008 whether blood cytokine levels can predict lung injury after radiation. Radiation is the main treatment for advanced lung cancer that cannot be removed by surgery. Its most serious dose-limiting harm is radiation pneumonitis, an inflammation of the lung.

Earlier reports had suggested that cytokine signals in plasma might flag who is at risk. The PLOS ONE paper tests that promise with a question in its title and data behind it. If such a test worked, doctors could tailor dose and watch high-risk patients more closely.
plos-pone-0002998:
Veronika Butin-Israeli, Dotan Uzi, Mahmoud Abd-El-Latif and co-authors used empty virus shells to protect mouse kidneys in 2008. Viruses trigger host defense and survival pathways during infection, but using real viruses for therapy is hampered by their harmful effects. SV40 capsids without DNA offer the trigger without the genome.

These DNA-free particles induced stress responses, survival pathways, and a pause in apoptosis, the authors report. Mice were protected from acute renal failure. Published in PLOS ONE, the approach tries to borrow a virus's alarm signals while leaving its dangers behind. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003098:
Gilberto Paz-Filho, Talin Babikian, Robert Asarnow and co-authors reported leptin treatment improving cognitive development in 2008. Leptin changes brain structure, neuron excitability, and synaptic plasticity, and it regulates feeding circuits. Its effects on how a child's learning and thinking develop were unknown.

Leptin replacement improved cognitive development, the title states, in the case or cases studied. Published in PLOS ONE, leptin deficiency is rare but revealing: a hormone known for satiety also shapes the developing mind. The finding widens what replacement therapy should be assessed for. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003198: Binh An Diep and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 on a toxin in community MRSA, the drug-resistant staph bacterium spread outside hospitals. The title states its subject: what part Panton-Valentine leukocidin plays in how this bacterium causes disease. No abstract text beyond the title was supplied, so this record states no findings.
plos-pone-0003298:
Christopher D. Fiorillo proposes a general theory of neural computation in this single-author 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Although there has been tremendous progress in understanding the mechanics of the nervous system, there has not been a general theory of its computational function. The author presents a theory that relates established biophysical properties of single generic neurons to principles of computation.

The theory is based on prediction by single neurons, as the title states. Readers get an attempt to ground brain computation in what one neuron can do, rather than in abstract networks alone. Single neuron prediction, if right, would simplify many models of learning.
plos-pone-0007398: Resveratrol, the compound found in grapes and red wine, has long been linked to lower prostate cancer risk, but how it works was unclear. This study shows it turns down the activity of the androgen receptor, a protein that drives prostate tumor growth. By mapping exactly where resveratrol hits this pathway, the work gives a concrete mechanism for a widely reported protective effect.
plos-pone-0007498: A cell signaling chain called MEK/ERK usually helps RNA viruses copy themselves — but hepatitis C breaks the rule. This study found that blocking MEK/ERK actually boosted hepatitis C replication and virus production. The surprise reveals that this virus relates to the host's signaling machinery differently than its viral cousins.
plos-pone-0007598: A companion study to the dendrite work above, this paper nails down the mechanism: the COP9 signalosome limits nerve-branch growth by destroying a protein called Kelch through a Cullin3-dependent pathway. Kelch crosslinks the cell's actin skeleton, so its controlled removal prunes branches. The finding connects a general protein-recycling system to precise brain wiring.
plos-pone-0007698: Glowing nanocrystals slipped into the freshwater animal Hydra revealed the creature's hidden doorways. This study used the particles to map regulated entry points into and between Hydra's cells. Beyond imaging, the finding shows nanoparticles can actively probe how simple animals manage their boundaries.
plos-pone-0007798: Keloids are raised scars that grow like benign tumors, unique to human skin. This study found they harbor tumor-like stem cells governed by an inflammatory niche driven by IL-17 and IL-6. The finding suggests even benign overgrowths obey the rules of the tumor microenvironment.
plos-pone-0007898: What predicts a child's thinking ability in Uganda? This study identified the socioeconomic factors most tied to cognition in Ugandan children. The findings guide where community interventions — nutrition, schooling, health — can do the most good.
plos-pone-0007998: Aging muscles waste away, but ginkgo extract may rewind the clock. This study found the extract EGb 761 reactivated a youthful gene program in the muscles of sarcopenic rats. The transcriptional reprogramming suggests a botanical route to fighting age-related frailty.
plos-pone-0008098: Silkworms' immune response to a killer bacterium was surveyed genome-wide. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Huang and colleagues tracked the host response of Bombyx mori during Bacillus bombyseptieus infection. The spore-forming pathogen was first isolated from dead silkworms. The genome-wide readout reveals how the valuable insect fights back.
plos-pone-0008198: A bone-growth signal was caught steering cells by a shortcut. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Perron and Dodd showed that two BMP receptor subunits, ActRIIA and BMPRII, are selectively needed for BMP7-triggered cell turning without Smad4. The rapid reorientation runs on membrane-local events, not the classic gene-switching route. The shortcut explains how cells pivot fast toward bone signals. The receptor split points to druggable targets in the fast pathway.
plos-pone-0008298: The fly's circadian clock runs on a neuropeptide called PDF. This study knocked it down in specific neuron subsets to map which cells drive which rhythmic behaviors. The anatomical dissection reveals the clock's wiring diagram.
plos-pone-0008398: Height genes were tested across ancestries. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Shriner's team checked 152 height-linked variants for transferability across human populations. Most finds came from European and East Asian groups. The cross-population fine-mapping shows which travel well. The results make gene scores fairer worldwide.
plos-pone-0008498: A fly's energy dial got a fuller manual. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Iijima's team showed CREB works in both brain and body tissues to set energy stores and feeding in Drosophila. The gene switch tunes fat and sugar handling. Tests in single tissues split its jobs. The fly work shows how animals balance their fuel.
plos-pone-0008598: Barley's rust resistance got a gene-expression map. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Chen's team ran eQTL analysis of partial resistance to Puccinia hordei in barley. Durable partial resistance beats fragile R genes. The expression map finds the loci. The map aids breeding tougher barley.
plos-pone-0008698: Heartbeat got a potassium-channel clue. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Imlach's team found BK channels regulate heart rate in rodents. The heart's electrical choreography needed the channel's role. The rhythm effect was measured. The clue informs cardiac biology.
plos-pone-0008798: Booze's brain-dock effect got a tag-removal twist. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Qiang's team found booze lifts a methyl tag off the NMDA dock gene, raising its readout. The tag-removal trick was mapped. The twist feeds addiction science.
plos-pone-0008898: Alzheimer's cortex got a microRNA-mRNA double read. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Nunez-Iglesias's team jointly profiled miRNA and mRNA in Alzheimer's cortex. The altered regulation was mapped. The double read informs dementia science.
plos-pone-0008998: Address-less homes got a map guess. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Curriero's team guessed map spots for address-less homes with fill-in math. The gap-filler was checked on real data. The guess aids health-map science.
plos-pone-0009098: Lung goo got a germ-film buster. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Gakhar's team found PLUNC lung goo busts germ films. The spit-out defender was mapped in airways. The buster feeds breathing care. The goo fights the films that clog airways.
plos-pone-0009198: Brain's tiny helpers got a gene roll call. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Koirala and Corfas read single cerebellum helper cells gene by gene. The new helper genes were listed. The roll call feeds brain science.
plos-pone-0009298: Heartbeat wiring got a variable-expression story. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Leoni's team linked variable Nav1.5 expression to conduction-disease penetrance in Scn5a mice. The allele-dosage mechanism was mapped. The story feeds cardiac genetics.
plos-pone-0011398: Lymph nodes are the immune system's main bases, but long-lasting inflammation makes the body build makeshift ones right inside sick organs. This research paper compares the immune responses launched from these improvised sites against the standard kind. Finding clear differences in their responses helps explain how local immune hubs shape diseases from arthritis to organ transplant rejection.
plos-pone-0011498: NELF was cast as a brake on gene transcription, pausing the copying machine mid-gene. This research paper finds it can also potentiate — boost — transcription in the Drosophila embryo. The flip from brake to accelerator reveals a two-faced regulator, complicating the simple story of how genes get switched on.
plos-pone-0011598: Cystic fibrosis stems from broken CFTR, and runaway inflammation scars patients' lungs. This research paper shows that normal CFTR suppresses NF-kB-driven inflammatory signaling. The finding reveals the healthy protein moonlights as an inflammation brake — lost in the disease.
plos-pone-0011698: Ecologists love a stats tool called hierarchical partitioning — but it may lean one way. This research paper measures that lean in the free public software. The bias check matters because real land and wildlife decisions rest on the tool's answers.
plos-pone-0011798: The enzyme cdc25C drives cells into division, working from separate pools. This research paper finds each pool wears different phosphate tags and parks in different spots of dividing human cells. The zoned control reveals how mitosis is timed with precision.
plos-pone-0011898: Ancient Nordic bones carry genetic stories of migration and survival. This research paper measures genetic diversity among ancient Nordic populations from old burial sites. The ancient DNA reveals how northern peoples moved, mixed, and endured across Scandinavia through the ages.
plos-pone-0011998: Mosasaurs were giant sea lizards — and one rare fossil reveals convergence. This research paper draws lessons on convergent evolution in water-dwelling tetrapods from the remarkable fossil. The ancient swimmer shows unrelated lineages solving the same watery problems in the sea.
plos-pone-0012098: Muscular dystrophy mice carry a microRNA clue. This research paper studies how miR-222 modulates the β1-syntrophin protein in mdx mice. The microRNA-protein link reveals a new lever on sick muscle for researchers today and always — hope for patients tomorrow and beyond.

plos-pone-0358698: The liver’s methionine cycle fuels metabolism, and the PPARγ protein helps run it. This paper mapped PPARγ-dependent and -independent regulation of methionine-cycle genes in fasted and diet-induced obese mice. The regulatory map clarifies how fasting and obesity rewire liver chemistry differently.
plos-pone-0356598: Alcohol-induced mental and behavioral disorders rarely travel alone. Drawing on Korea’s national hospital discharge injury survey, this paper mapped their comorbidities — the conditions that cluster alongside. The evidence guides doctors toward integrated treatment instead of chasing each diagnosis separately.
plos-pone-0347398: Flying taxis need networks — and green ones. This paper showed how 6G integrated perception and networking, with a dynamic sleep strategy for eVTOL wireless systems, can push the low-altitude economy toward carbon neutrality. The sleep strategy cuts energy waste during the quiet hours when the skies are empty.
plos-pone-0357098: The deep sea hides our trash. This ROV survey revealed marine litter in the Mar del Plata Submarine Canyon in the southwestern Atlantic — out of sight, hidden in the deep. The findings document how far human waste reaches, in a place almost no human will ever visit.
plos-pone-0357498: The choroid plexus — the brain’s cerebrospinal fluid factory — changes size near tumors. This paper studied choroid plexus volume variation in patients with gliomas and related tumors, linking it to tumor characteristics. The volume shifts may become a valuable new imaging marker for diagnosis and monitoring.
plos-pone-0354798: How do you measure a population’s dissatisfaction with collective decisions? ElecMeter is a proposed index for evaluating dissatisfaction in social decision-making. The metric gives democracies, committees, and organizations a rigorous way to quantify discontent instead of merely sensing it.
plos-pone-0357598: The Yangtze River Delta’s relentless urban sprawl threatens the region’s ecological foundations. This paper assessed ecological sensitivity and sustainable spatial planning across the highly urbanized plain using AHP-GIS and geodetector methods. The analysis guides urbanization that leaves room for nature to survive.
plos-pone-0355298: Social trust protects against depression — but traditional gender attitudes change the equation. This Seoul study examined social trust and depression among young adults, with traditional gender role attitudes as moderator. The interplay reveals cultural nuances that one-size-fits-all mental health models miss.
plos-pone-0356498: Smarter optimization algorithms can decarbonize supply chains. This three-term conjugate gradient method with a new descent structure tackles both unconstrained optimization and low-carbon supply chain design. The mathematics finds better solutions faster — with a smaller carbon footprint as the prize.
plos-pone-0356398: Young Zambians need sexual and reproductive health services that actually reach them. This place-based study co-produced access with young people through digital tools and vending machine-enabled innovation. The co-designed approach meets youth where they already are — on their phones and streets.
plos-pone-0355198: When food prices soar, the poor don’t just eat less — they eat worse. This paper tracked rising food prices and widening nutrition gaps in Mexico, comparing the cost of nutrient-dense foods against ultra-processed ones before, during, and after COVID-19. The price trajectories reveal exactly how the pandemic priced healthy eating out of reach for millions of Mexican families, and whether the gap has closed since.
plos-pone-0356798: Seafarers and ship crews face unique health risks with minimal support. This scoping review mapped digital health promotion, prevention, and health literacy measures available to crews on cargo and passenger ships. The review reveals a largely neglected population — and the digital tools that could reach them at sea.
plos-pone-0341298: Does feeling that society is unfair change what policies people want? This paper investigated the relationship between perceived inequality and policy preferences. The findings map how subjective experiences of unfairness — not just objective gaps — drive demand for redistribution. Democracy’s policy debates run on perceptions as much as facts.
plos-pone-0355598: Fenugreek — a valuable spice and medicinal crop — needs optimal planting geometry. The agronomic findings give farmers the spacing recipe for maximum harvest.
plos-pone-0356198: Macrophages that flip between inflammatory states reshape how triple-negative breast cancer hides from immunity. The findings reveal the tumor microenvironment as a therapeutic target in its own right.
plos-pone-0355698: Hemodialysis patients’ gut microbiomes are profoundly disturbed — with consequences for their survival. plos-pone-0355998: Global Geoparks must balance beauty with conservation — and landscape quality can be measured. This paper evaluated visual landscape quality using an SBE–GIS coupled model. plos-pone-0354298: Identifying winter wheat in desert oases from space demands fusing satellite data types. plos-pone-0355498: Trust in public health authorities — the currency of pandemic response — needs precise measurement. This paper measured it in the United States using item response theory. plos-pone-0336198: A women-led community center in Tripoli, Lebanon — can it build social cohesion amid sectarian tension? This pilot randomized controlled trial tested the impact. plos-pone-0355398: Coffee and tea cultures — Qingdao versus Jinan — evolved differently from 2018 to 2024. This paper compared the dynamics of their cultural spaces. The findings reveal how two Chinese cities brewed distinct beverage identities — a case study in urban cultural geography.
plos-pone-0354898: Power line insulators crack — and drones must spot the defects. plos-pone-0348698: Rewilded elephants — returned to the wild after captivity — cope in ways worth comparing to wild herds. This paper compared their behavioral and physiological adaptive mechanisms. plos-pone-0354198: Type 2 diabetes’ economic burden — stratified by social determinants — reveals who pays most. This systematic review synthesized that burden. The findings show diabetes taxes the disadvantaged disproportionately — the economic case for health equity.

Ludwig Blau published the first systematic survey of ancient Jewish magic in 1898, in German. His study drew on rabbinic literature, inscriptions, and archaeological finds. Amulets, angel names, and exorcisms all fall within his map.

Gawain and Perceval ride out on quests that fill thirty-five branches, or chapters, of the tale. They meet violence, visions, and marvels that test faith as much as courage. Castles, hermits, and strange beasts crowd the road. Readers who know only Malory's Grail will find this one fiercer and more fevered, closer to a dream than to a chronicle.

A giant green knight rides into Camelot at Christmas and offers a game. Any man may strike him once with an axe, if Gawain will take the same blow in a year. Gawain accepts, cuts off the stranger's head, and watches him pick it up and ride away. What follows tests Gawain's courage, honesty, and honor at the Green Chapel.
